scenes.text: Store a linear-attention state in BF16, and Qwen3.5-9B falls from 87.9 to 72.1 on AIME. Why?
scenes.say: Store a linear attention state in BF16, and Qwen three point five, nine B, falls from eighty-seven point nine to seventy-two point one on a math benchmark. Why?

scenes.headline: How LeapQuant keeps a recurrent state in 8 bits
scenes.sub: Round less often, then make each rounding cheaper
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Ludo! LeapQuant stores this state in eight bits and keeps full precision accuracy. Here is how.

scenes.title: A state read every token
scenes.sub: Why the recurrent state is a bandwidth bill
scenes.say: Chapter one. A state read every token.

scenes.title: One decode step of a Gated DeltaNet head

steps.say: Each Gated DeltaNet head keeps one matrix, a hundred and twenty-eight square. A new token brings a key, a correction and a decay.

steps.term: Delta rule: write only what the memory gets wrong
steps.say: The update decays the matrix, then adds one rank-one write: the key, times what the memory got wrong about that key. That is the delta rule.
Then the whole matrix goes back to memory. Every token, every head, every layer.

steps.note: 144 MiB per stream on Qwen3.8-27B in FP32
steps.say: On Qwen three point eight, twenty-seven B, that is a hundred and forty-four mebibytes per stream. Halve the bytes and you halve the bill.

scenes.title: Every token is a decay and one write

parts.note: decay: forget a little of the old state
parts.say: First the decay. A slow head forgets a tiny fraction per token.

parts.note: one rank-one write: key times correction
parts.say: Then one rank-one write. Each write is small next to the state it lands on.

scenes.title: Why rounding piles up
scenes.sub: Small changes vanish under a coarse grid
scenes.say: Chapter two. Why rounding piles up.

scenes.title: Round every token, or once per window

legend: One entry of the state, decaying slowly
Each change is under half a level, so it never moves
Exact updates inside the window, one rounding at its end
Same bits, a fraction of the drift

steps.say: Follow one entry of the state as it slowly decays. The faint lines are the only values a low-bit format can store.

steps.term: Half a level: smaller changes round away
steps.say: Round it after every token. Each change is smaller than half a level, so it rounds straight back, and the stored value never moves. In BF16, a decay of zero point nine nine nine is erased completely.
LeapQuant holds the stored state fixed, buffers sixteen tokens of updates in higher precision, and applies them exactly. It rounds once, at the window's end.
A few roundings instead of one per token, and nothing small is thrown away.
The paper measured this on Qwen three point five over sixty-four thousand tokens. Rounded every token, INT8 and BF16 both drift away.
Rounded once per window, the error stays near the floor, and LeapQuant's line is lowest of all.

scenes.title: Lift outliers, smooth the rest
scenes.say: Chapter three. Lift the outliers, smooth the rest.

scenes.title: One outlier sets the whole grid

params.paper: one Qwen3.5-9B head, peak over median, Figure 6
legend: Two outlier rows set the step: small entries get almost no levels
Lift the outliers out as rank-one tokens: the grid gets finer
Divide each row by the root of its mean size: finer again

steps.say: Here is one value channel. Its scale is set by its largest entry, so two outlier rows leave ordinary entries on a grid far too coarse.

steps.term: Compensator Token: an outlier kept as a token
steps.say: LeapQuant subtracts the strongest rank-one pieces. Each has the shape of a token's write, so it rides in the window buffer, kept in FP16.
Smoothing then divides each key row by the square root of its mean size, and multiplies back when it reads.
On one real Qwen three point five head, the peak falls from a hundred and seventy-six times the median, to forty-seven, to five point three.
The authors animate the same idea. Outlier rows and columns lift out as Compensator Tokens, and the rest is rescaled row by row until it is flat.
The paper's picture of a window: residual, plus Compensator Tokens, plus buffered real tokens, add up to the full state.
The compensators sit in the same list as real tokens, so the kernel needs no second path.
A window starts from the stored state: an INT8 residual, its scales and four FP16 tokens. One point one nine bytes per value, against four.
Each decode step reads that state and the buffer, and appends its own key and correction. It writes no state.
After sixteen tokens, the kernel rebuilds the full state.
It fits four new Compensator Tokens, subtracts them, and smooths the rows.
Then it rounds once, and the next window begins.

scenes.title: Does it hold up?
scenes.sub: Accuracy, speed, and what the code ships
scenes.say: Chapter four. Does it hold up?

scenes.title: AIME 2026 on Qwen3.5-9B, INT8 state
scenes.say: The paper's ablation. INT8 rounded every token scores seven point one. The window lifts it to eighty-two point four, compensators to eighty-six point six, and smoothing to full precision's eighty-seven point nine.

scenes.title: One layer, against the FP32 kernel

steps.say: Kernel throughput for one layer. At batch five hundred and twelve, Gated DeltaNet runs two point six eight times faster on a B200.
And four point two five times on an RTX fifty ninety, the best cell. End to end, the paper averages one point five seven times.

scenes.title: What the released code ships
scenes.say: The open code is narrower than the paper.

items.say: It writes the low-bit state inside the full precision slot, so it saves traffic, not memory.
It refuses prefix caching, which is where the paper measured its memory savings.
And its kernels use copy engines that arrived with Hopper, so an RTX thirty ninety is out.

scenes.text: A low-bit recurrent state works if you round it rarely and make each rounding small.
scenes.say: A low-bit recurrent state works, if you round it rarely, and make each rounding small.

recap: Rounding every token freezes slow decays
Compensators and smoothing shrink each rounding
scenes.say: Round rarely, lift the outliers, smooth the rest. See you next time!
